The content covers basic financial vocabulary and how the finance world functions. Thanks to this course, I finally understand the financial part of news reports.

There are two 1.5 hour long classes per week, attendance recommended. The professor goes through the slides, asks questions, and sometimes makes us have group discussions. It is recommended to take notes as some explanations are only said out loud and not written down on the slides. There is also a TA present in the room, whom you can also ask questions to at the end of class.
sections.teaching: Ms. Lafon-Vinais is one of the best professors I have had at UST. She explains well and makes the classes interactive so it doesn't make you fall asleep. Even if you don't understand a concept right away, she is happy to answer questions related to the course or even finance in general after class.
sections.grading:
Attendence is graded. All you need is to participate once per class for a total of 12 classes to get 6%. Otherwise, you can also contribute to the discussion board on Canvas (0.5% per contribution I think). Another 4% can be obtained by participating in 80% of the total iPRS questions in class.

As an engineering student (no econ or finance background), I found it easy to get an A- in this course. I got just above the mean for the midterm, and got above 80% for each of the quizzes. The final exam scores were not published.
sections.workload:
4 online quizzes on Canvas, group assignment, group presentation, midterm, final.

If you've paid attention in class, the online quizzes should be relatively easy. You just need to keep aside a list of the formulae (if any) and a calculator in case you come across a calculation-related question. Each quiz only takes about half an hour.

The group assignment is about finding an article and a short video about a certain topic you are assigned to. There is no need to analyse or study them. Only 2 links are needed per group. This takes about a few minutes to possibly half an hour depending on how well you know your assigned topic.

The presentation is done with the same group as the previous assignment. 3 minute presentation about market news and a short Q&A. Not everyone needs to speak, but everyone needs to be present. This should take a total of about 1-2 hours to prepare (if you are preparing both the slides and the Q&A, and your team members aren't doing much work).

Midterm and final exams are non-cumulative. The midterm is about the first half of the syllabus and the final about the rest. You are allowed to bring as many paper notes as you want (written, typed, screenshotted...). I would recommend being familiar with your notes or have some sort of system to quickly find the info you need since there is no time to go through each page of your notes for each question. They don't take too long to prepare, especially since most of the questions come from the quizzes.

sections.content:
This course covers a practical overview of the financial system, focusing heavily on financial institutions rather than the deep mechanics of stock and bond markets. The weekly schedule is structured as follows:

Week 1: Introduction; overview of financial markets  
Week 2: Foundations of Interest Rates Parts 1 and 2
Week 3: Financial intermediation; types of FIs (Part I)  
Week 4: Financial intermediation; types of FIs (Part II)  
Week 5: The sell-side: commercial banks (Part I)  
Week 6: The sell-side: commercial banks (Part II)  
Week 7: The sell-side: investment banking  
Week 8: Fundamentals of pricing and valuation  
Week 9: The buy-side: institutional investors and other FIs (Part I)  
Week 10: The buy-side: institutional investors and other FIs (Part II)  
Week 11: The buy-side: alternatives  
Week 12: Financial & Banking Regulation (if time allows)  
Week 13: Central banking & monetary policy (if time allows)  

Maybe it will be quite fun for the non-SBM students, but I already learnt most of the things in my previous courses. But still recommend you to reg, whether for a good grade or a brief understanding in finance market
sections.teaching: The teaching quality is quite good. Professor Veronique Lafon-Vinais teaches at a very manageable, slow pace and explains concepts clearly. Because she breaks down the foundational aspects of financial systems without rushing, the lectures are super friendly and accessible for non-SBM (School of Business and Management) students who might not have a prior background in finance.
sections.grading:
The assessment scheme in the syllabus is broken down as follows:  

Mid-term Exam (Exam I): 25%  

Final Exam (Exam II): 25%  

Online Quizzes (4 total): 20% (5% each)  

Group Assignment & Peer Evaluation (2 total): 20% (10% each)  

Class Participation (via iPRS & discussions): 10%  

Honestly, the grading is really good and it is very easy to secure an A-range grade, especially for SBM students. I didn't have to put a massive amount of effort into studying for the mid-term and final exams; simply attending the lectures consistently is more than enough to handle the assessment papers. A huge plus is that the exams and quizzes are entirely multiple-choice (MCQ) or True/False format, which keeps the testing straightforward.
sections.workload: The workload for this course is super light. There are 4 online quizzes and 2 group assignments in total, but each assignment only took about 1 to 2 hours to complete. When it comes to exam revision, you don't need to overthink it. Just doing the exercises and the quiz are entirely enough to prepare you well.

1. Intro, an overview of financial markets
- Financial statements, financial system, financial markets, players of FMs, classification of FMs
2. Foundations of interest rates [Calculation topic]
- Discounted cash flow concept (Present and future value)
- Perpetuities, annuities, bonds and short-term debt instrument calculations
3. Financial intermediation, types of financial intermediaries
4. Sell-side: Commercial banks
- Bank management: Liquidity, asset, liability and capital management
- Types of risk in banking, bank performance, bank organisation, issues in banking
5. Sell-side: Investment banking
6. Fundamentals of pricing and valuation [Calculation topic]
- Equity valuation, dividend-discount model DDM
7. Buy-side: Institutional investors and other financial intermediaries
- Insurance, pension and retirement funds, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds ETFs
8. Buy-side: Alternatives
- Sovereign wealth funds SWFs, angel investors, venture capital, private equity, hedge fund
9. Financial & Banking regulation (If time allows, which we didn't teach)
10. Central banking & Monetary policy (If time allows, which we didn't teach)

A lot of slides and words for each topic, but if you follow along in class, you will be fine. Also, since it is open notes, you just need to make sure to have well-organised notes that you can search through quickly.

As someone without prior knowledge of or any interest in any of these topics, the content is not challenging and even is useful in understanding financial events occurring globally.
sections.teaching:

sections.content:
I'd say the content of this course is divided into 2 parts: quantitative and factual. For the quantitative part, we learn some basic knowledge about discounted cash flows and stock valuation. For the factual part, there's a lot to memorize, including definitions and financial regulations. For more details, please refer to other reviews.
Even though you do not have previous knowledge in finance, you won't find it too difficult to understand the content and you should be able to catch up with the progress as long as you have an interest in finance/the financial industry and keep going over the lecture notes.
sections.teaching:
She is very passionate and she likes interacting with students. She encourages discussions and she would walk through the lecture hall to ask students to give their opinions. Her voice is sharp and sometimes she is funny, which would make you awake. I enjoyed her lessons.
However, I only give a "B" because she did not include most of the content that would appear in quizzes and exams in the lecture notes. Therefore, if you want to get a good grade, make sure that you rewatch every lecture video and copy down every single word she said so that you won't miss out anything.
Btw, the TA is so nice and he replies to emails in a timely manner.
sections.grading:
Participation: 10%, all of which are from iPRS. You don't have to get the answer correct, so don't worry even though you don't know the answer. However, there are quite a number of iPRS every lesson, so make sure that you have answered all of them.
Online quizzes: 20%, 5% each, one per month.
Group assignments: 20%, 10% each.
Mid-term exam and final exam: 25% each.

All questions in the quizzes and exams are in the form of MC or T/F. One good thing is that you are allowed to bring your devices and refer to the lecture notes during the mid-term exam and final exam, so you don't have to memorize everything. However, the topics covered in every quiz/exam involve hundreds of pages and time is limited, so you have to familiarize yourself with the lecture notes in order to search for the answers asap during quizzes/exams. If you don't have "sources" but you want to get a good grade, do spare some time to watch her lecture videos and copy down everything she said so that you won't feel shocked when something that is not mentioned in the lecture notes appears in the quizzes/exams.

This isn't the course you take to learn how to trade stocks. That's other courses.

sections.workload:
IPRS - IPRS in class almost every lesson, you don't have to get the correct answer but you must answer. She will explain the answer.

Chat/Breakout Room - We only had two breakout rooms. She tells u to go discuss something then come back and one person per group share with the class. If your group did nothing pray u can bs or just rephrase what the other groups said. Unless your group 1 in which case good luck. For chat don't ask stupid stupid things or the questions where you're actually showing off your financial knowledge. Prof and TA will sense it from a mile away. Just IPRS is fine for participation points. IPRS questions actually show up again in the quizzes.

Quizzes & Exam - Time limit (hour to hour and a half if i remember correctly) TF, MCQ and fill ins. There are a lot more T/F and MCQ then fill ins but the fill ins are worth a lot of points and are math questions. She provides a spreadsheet for the formula so the trick is figuring out from the word question which formula to use. Open Book quiz.

A lot of the questions are actually only quizzes online.  

Groupwork - Two group projects. One was to record a presentation and send and another was to find news videos corresponding to a prompt. These are early in the class so ask her questions and get her to check before the hand in. You can ask if the article link you chose seems ok. Take the opportunity of her kindness in this matter.Also, a lot less work than it sounds like.

COURSE DESCRIPTION ：
This course aims to provide  the participants with basic and practical knowledge in the structure and function of the financial system. We examine the  role, objectives and function of financial  regulation,  the evolving role of central banking and monetary policy and the implications and consequences on financial institutions and markets. Throughout the course we link prevalent economic theories to market realities. Topics covered include: the fundamentals  of interest rates and  basic pricing  of financial assets,  including basic concepts such as  cash flows, the time value of money and  the risk-return  tradeoff; the  structure  and  function of the financial system, the  role and the types of  financial institutions and financial intermediaries; the goals of financial and banking regulations, the organization of central banks and the role of monetary policy. There will be a strong focus on financial institutions, understanding the role that the different types of firms play and how they interact. This course does NOT go into details of various markets for stocks, bonds and other securities, which are covered in other finance courses.

JUST A LOT OF HARD FACTS TO RECITE!

This course gives you an overview on financial market such as overview on commercial & investment banks, interests rate calculations and financial regulations. This course can give you a brief overview on what finance is about, but I feel like there are too much stuff to recite (Expect >70 slides per chapter) and it gets kinda boring. It doesn't matter whether you've studies BAFS in DSE as almost all chapters are new stuff.

===Content=== (* involves calculation)
1. Introduction to Financial Markets
*2. Foundations of Interest Rates I
*3. Foundations of Interest Rates II
4. Financial Intermediation
5. The Sell Side: Commercial Banks
6. The Sell Side: Investment Banks

*8. Stock Valuation

----Final Exam (Ch. 6 [2nd part] ~10)----

===General Comments===
Basically this course introduces what financial services do, like banks, hedge funds, mutual funds and etc. The professor didn't go too deep into those and introduces us some common technical jargon.

However, I don't like that this course needs so much memorization! Each chapter has around 20~40 slides that have key points to remember, and sometimes we need to recite BORING stuff like which regulation does what thing. Would love to see more calculation in this course rather than factual stuff.

I would recommend this course to business students because the calculation concepts will be taught again in FINA2303 so it's good to have some background knowledge
sections.teaching:
The professor tries to make the lesson atmosphere relaxed and fun. She loves asking students questions and run around in the lecture hall to stuff microphone to students.

I think she's fine when explaining concepts. She would give basic explanation to technical terms and make additional notes. What I don't like about her is that she only explains HALF of the technical jargon! It's very easy to get lost in lessons as she skip lecture slides so fast that I cannot digest. You need to look out the remaining jargon in Investopedia mainly

She also loves to go off-topic in lessons to introduce you current issues in finance or a scenario problem. This gives you some more insight, but personally I would love her explain the jargon clearer instead. It's kinda boring when she does that.
